spine.core_thesis: I've spent three years closing mid-market fleet deals at Motive — including head-to-head wins and losses against Samsara — so I already know the objections, the buyer personas, and the platform gaps on both sides; joining Samsara means I can sell from the stronger side of the story I've watched win.
spine.company_hook: Three years closing mid-market fleet deals at Motive — including direct head-to-head against Samsara — mean I arrive already knowing the buyer objections, the platform comparison, and what Samsara's unified hardware-plus-cloud story actually does in a deal room; I want to sell from the stronger side of that story.

positioning_frame.frame_statement: Leverage lived, deal-level competitive experience against Samsara to demonstrate immediate ramp value and credible platform conviction from day one.

cards.label: Tell me about yourself
cards.content:
## Quick take
Three years closing fleet deals at Motive means I've already lost deals to Samsara — and I know exactly why. --- ## 30-second version Yeah, so basically I've spent the last three years as a mid-market AE at Motive, closing fleet telematics and AI dashcam deals to trucking and construction fleets across Texas and the Southwest. I closed **just over $1.2 million in new ARR** across that run , mostly 25-to-200 unit fleets. And honestly, the most useful thing I did in that job was compete against Samsara on almost every deal. I know the objections, I know the buyer personas, I know where Motive wins and where it doesn't. So coming to Samsara as an AE feels less like starting over and more like switching to the side I kept losing to. --- ## Full answer (~60 seconds) So over the last three years I've closed **just over $1.2 million in new ARR at Motive** , mostly mid-market trucking and construction fleets, 25 to 200 units. Full-cycle motion the whole time: outbound prospecting, discovery with safety directors and fleet ops managers, technical scoping, all the way through close. And look , I think the most honest way to describe my time at Motive is that I got really good at competing against Samsara. Almost every deal had a Samsara evaluation running in parallel. I won some. I lost some. And when I lost, I usually knew why. Actually , one deal I want to mention. Last October I closed a **120-truck construction fleet in Texas at $42k ARR** that had told me four weeks in they were leaning Samsara because of the site-visibility module , a capability gap on our side. I pulled in our SE, built an API integration story around their existing yard system, and got a reference call going with a comparable carrier. Closed it. But I remember thinking afterward , if I'd been selling Samsara, that objection never comes up. I started at ADP as an SDR before Motive, booking meetings with HR and payroll buyers , that's where I got the outbound reps in. But the last three years is really where the deal complexity came from. **Which is why I'm genuinely excited about this AE role at Samsara** , I'm not walking in cold on the product or the market. I've watched Samsara win from the other side of the table. --- ## Key proof points - **$1.2M ARR closed** across mid-market trucking and construction at Motive
- **$42k ARR construction expansion** won head-to-head against Samsara
- **3 years of direct Samsara competitive reps** , objections, personas, platform gaps --- ## If they dig deeper **"Why are you leaving Motive?"**
Honestly it's less about leaving and more about conviction. I've watched Samsara win deals on platform breadth that Motive genuinely couldn't match , the connected operations story, one platform across vehicles, equipment, and sites. I want to sell the fuller story. That's a deliberate choice, not an escape. **"You've been on the Motive side , why should we trust your product conviction about Samsara?"**
Yeah, that's fair. I think the most credible conviction comes from watching something beat you repeatedly and figuring out why. The 73% crash-reduction stat , I've had buyers cite that to me by name at the COO level. I've had to answer it from the other side. I know it's real, and I know what makes it defensible. That's not something you pick up from a product sheet. --- ## Make it yours - [Your actual quota attainment percentage , e.g., "I was at 112% for the year" , if you have it, drop it right after the $1.2M line to anchor the credibility early]
- [If you have a specific moment from a Samsara loss , a deal you didn't close, what the buyer said, what you learned , drop it in the Full Answer after the Hill & Sons win. One loss makes the win feel more real.]

cards.label: Why Samsara?
cards.content:
## Quick take
I've spent three years selling against Samsara — now I want to sell from the side that wins on platform breadth. --- ## 30-second version Yeah, so honestly the reason is pretty simple. I've been at Motive for three years closing mid-market fleet deals, and I've gone head-to-head with Samsara more times than I can count. And I've won some, I've lost some. But the losses taught me something , when a buyer is running mixed operations, vehicles plus yard equipment plus site visibility, **Samsara's unified platform just covers more ground** than what I was selling. I kept coming up against that ceiling. So I'd rather be on the side where I'm not hitting it. --- ## Full answer (~60 seconds) Yeah, so the honest answer is that I've been studying Samsara from the other side of the table for three years. At Motive I was selling into mid-market trucking and construction , 25 to 200 unit fleets , and I ran into Samsara constantly. And I want to be real: I lost deals to you guys. One that sticks with me was a 120-truck construction fleet in Texas. The safety director told me point-blank they were leaning Samsara because **they didn't want to manage two vendor relationships, and Samsara's site and equipment visibility covered their yard** , a place where Motive just didn't have parity yet. I ended up closing that one by pulling in an SE and running a reference call, but I had to work twice as hard to get there. The thing I actually couldn't argue with , I mean, I tried to reframe it, but deep down I knew it was real , was the platform breadth story. **When a fleet is running vehicles, equipment, and workers on one job site, the Connected Operations Cloud actually covers all of it.** Motive is strong on the vehicle side. But Samsara goes wider. And then I looked at the FY25 safety report , **73% crash rate reduction across 2,600-plus fleets over 30 months** , that's not a one-off case study, that's proof at scale. That's the kind of number that a safety director can take to their CFO and actually close internal budget. So yeah. I know the objections buyers have. I know where competitors try to attack. I just want to be on the side where I'm telling the stronger story. --- ## Key proof points - **Lost a 120-truck deal mid-pitch** when site visibility gap surfaced , saw it firsthand
- Competed against Samsara across **[your number , e.g., 15–20] head-to-head deals** at Motive
- **73% crash reduction at 2,600+ fleets** , knew this number before this interview --- ## If they dig deeper **"What do you think Samsara's biggest competitive weakness is?"** Honestly? Price point, in smaller fleets. Sub-50 trucks, the platform breadth is a harder sell because they're not running mixed operations , they just need ELD and basic dashcam, and a cheaper point solution feels like enough. But in the mid-market sweet spot, 50 trucks and up, especially construction and mixed fleets, I don't think the breadth argument really has a good counter. **"Who do you think the ideal Samsara customer is?"** From what I've seen in deals , and I've sat across from these buyers , it's a fleet director or safety director at a construction or logistics company, probably 75 to 300 trucks, who's already past the 'do we need telematics' conversation and is now asking 'how do we consolidate vendors and get one view of everything.' That buyer is done shopping for features. They want a platform. That's exactly who Samsara wins with. --- ## Make it yours - **[Your head-to-head count]** , drop in roughly how many Samsara competitive deals you touched at Motive: *"I ran into Samsara on probably [15–20] deals over three years"*
- **[Your win/loss split]** , if you remember a rough ratio, it makes the answer feel more honest and specific: *"I'd say I won maybe [X] of those and lost [Y] , and the losses were almost always the same story"*
